name: Diego Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at seven, even at weekends, because my dad does. Weekdays are lectures in electrical engineering, circuits mostly, and a lab on Thursday where I actually enjoy myself. I live in student housing with five other lads, and I cook for them on Sundays because I can't stand takeaway. Saturdays I work at my uncle Marek's garage, changing tyres and doing basic electrics on cars. Dad is a welder, Mum cleans offices in the mornings, and they pay about half of my costs, with the rest coming from my garage wages and a bit of savings. I go to church with my family when I'm home, about twice a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds right to me. I've never trusted big promises from people who sell the thing. At the garage, my uncle Marek would say, good, a machine can't change a tyre when the customer's in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief. I picked electrical engineering because it's a proper trade with a degree on top, and I want to work with real equipment, not a screen. The thing I carry is money. The garage pays 60 a Saturday, and my parents have a mortgage, so every month is close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd keep my Saturday job, because I like it and it pays. I'd ask the department about a summer placement with an electrical contractor, since I'd rather learn on a real site. And I'd keep doing my work myself, without any shortcuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's how I'd want it to stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said every month is close. What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own spending, always. I don't spend much anyway, but I'd skip the coach trip home some weekends, which saves 25. I'd never ask Mum for more, because she's up at five to clean offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever think about what you'd do if the degree doesn't work out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go into an electrician's apprenticeship. There's no shame in it, and honestly in some ways I'd like it more. My dad always says a trade is something nobody can take away from you.

At the garage, a machine can't change a tyre when the customer's in a **hurry**.
think: It's a **relief**, because I wanted real equipment, not a screen.

do: Keep the **Saturday job** at my uncle's garage.
Ask the department about a **summer placement** with an electrical contractor.
Keep doing my work **myself**, without shortcuts.
feel: **Calm**, which is how I'd want it to stay.

fieldNote: Chose **electrical engineering** as a trade with a degree on top and wants real equipment.

An **apprenticeship** is a fallback he'd accept without shame.

steps.text: Keep working Saturdays at my uncle's garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the garage that people will still need honest workers who can fix things. I'd say it to my friends at church too, where the older men worry about their sons. Online, I'd say nothing, because I don't like shouting into a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I don't like it. The design side of my degree could shrink, and I'd hate to be the person who sits in front of a machine all day making decisions I don't understand. I'd want the part of the job where my hands are on the equipment, like commissioning, testing and fault-finding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean harder on the hands-on side. I'd seek a placement with a firm that installs and repairs electrical systems, and I'd keep the garage job. I wouldn't use the AI tools unless the university makes me, but I'd read about them, so I know what the lads on site might be using.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear a noise in the engine and you don't know yet what it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies that chase the cheapest option, and politicians who talk about the future but don't live in it. I'm not against progress. I'm against people losing their living and being told it's for the best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help someone like your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apprenticeships and training that employers actually pay for. Not handouts. Dad would never take one, but he'd take a chance to train for the next job.

steps.text: Apply for a placement with an electrical installation firm
Keep my Saturday garage job and learn fault-finding
Vote for candidates who back employer-paid apprenticeships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after each other, and that families and churches have to keep people together. I'd say politicians should stop talking and make jobs for people who need them. I wouldn't know what else to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened. If AI does most thinking work by 2028, my degree might be worth nothing by the time I finish. The robots come later, around 2031, so hands-on work lasts a bit longer, but I'm not sure my parents' work stays safe either. Dad's welding is exactly the kind of job robots will take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents the first Sunday, with the whole family. I'd get a full-time job during the summer, at the garage or on a building site, and save every pound. I might leave the degree and go for an electrician's apprenticeship, because a trade is at least something real. I'd also ask the priest and the church group what help there is for families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can't see how my parents pay the mortgage if both their jobs go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'll earn alongside him. I'm not going to make my dad pay for a degree that gives us nothing. He'd say no, finish it, and then he'd go quiet and stare at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to choose, yes. I'm not proud of the grades for show. A good job I can do with my hands is worth more to me than a piece of paper that doesn't open any doors.

say: Families and churches have to **keep people together**, and politicians should make jobs, not speeches.
I wouldn't know what else to say.
think: My degree might be **worth nothing** by the time I finish.
My dad's **welding** is exactly the job robots will take, so my parents' work isn't safe.

feel: **Alarmed**, because I can't see how my parents pay the mortgage if both jobs go.
S2.quote: I'm not going to make my dad pay for a degree that gives us nothing.
fieldNote: His fear is for **his parents'** mortgage as much as his own future.
Would **leave** the degree for an apprenticeship; trade skills feel more real.
Looks to **church** and family first for help.

steps.text: Hold a family talk the first Sunday after the news

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to get ready, so people should get ready. I'd tell my friends at church to teach the young a trade, and to keep savings for a rainy day. At the garage, I'd say nothing really changes about a punctured tyre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel more worried than I'd say. I'd graduate in 2029 or 2030, which is right before the main change. But I'd have a few years to put money aside and get the practical skills that last into 2034, when robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and spend the summers on site, so I can be a graduate who can also wire a panel. I'd save 3,000, or as close as I can. I'd help my parents pay down the mortgage a bit once I have a salary. And I'd probably learn how the tools work in third year, but only because I'd have to, not because I want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I know what to do. It's a bit like a long winter, where you know to cut the wood now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with five years, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd quit and take the trade right away. With five, I can finish and have the degree and the trade skills both. That feels fairer to my parents, who've put in so much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your younger cousin who's thinking about uni?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say go, but don't go blind. Get a summer job on site, learn from the old men, and keep your options open. A degree plus real skills is a strong hand.

fieldNote: Five years lets him keep **both** the degree and trade skills.

steps.text: Spend summers working on electrical sites
Put part of my first salary towards my parents' mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good length of time to prepare, and people shouldn't panic. I'd tell the younger lads to learn a trade and not wait to be told. At church I'd say we'll look after each other, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly steady. I'd be 28, working, maybe with a family of my own, and by 2039 the robots would be coming. I'd worry for Dad though. He'd be in his late fifties, with a body that's already tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a few years in an electrical firm, and save for a house. I'd help my parents so Dad can slow down before the robots arrive. And I'd keep a hands-on skill in reserve, like being a qualified electrician, so there's something to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. It's far enough off that I can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your mind about the tools by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everyone is using them, probably yes. I'd learn them the way I learned to drive, slowly and with someone beside me. I'm not afraid of them, I just don't want to rely on them before I understand them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from leaders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fair deal for people who work. Support for small firms, apprenticeships, and not letting big companies take all the gain. If the work changes, the pay and respect should still go to the people who do it.

At church I'd say we'll **look after each other**, same as always.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. My parents would still be paying the mortgage, I'd be halfway through a degree, and nobody would have the time to plan. What would help is quick, honest information, apprenticeships for people who need them, and keeping families together. The government shouldn't hand out money without a path to work, but it should help people reach one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think students like me are soft, and we're not. I get up at seven, I work Saturdays, and I'm doing my best. I'd just like someone to say what's really coming, in plain words.

headlineQuote: I'd just like someone to say what's really coming, in plain words.
portrait: Diego is an **18-year-old** electrical engineering student, who works Saturdays at his uncle's garage and never uses AI.
His dad is a **welder** and his mum cleans offices, so family money and the mortgage are his main pressure.
He is **traditional**: work, apprenticeships, family and church over handouts, and a trade as a fallback.
He is calm in the slow worlds and **alarmed at two years**, when he'd leave the degree to protect his parents.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most: his parents' mortgage, a half-finished degree, and no time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: Quick, **honest information**, apprenticeships for people who need them, and a path to work rather than handouts.
